The journey of Ahmad ibn Fadlan, a member of an embassy sent by the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir from Baghdad to the king of the Volga Bulgars in 921 and 922. His written account is one of the best eyewitness sources on the peoples of the steppe and the Volga in that age.

The Bulgar king had recently become Muslim. He asked the caliph for teachers of the faith and for money to build a fort, as he was a vassal of the Jewish Khazars and wanted to be free of them. The embassy travelled through Iran and Khwarazm and then across the steppe in winter. Ibn Fadlan described the Oghuz Turks and other peoples on the way.

His most famous pages are on the Rus, Scandinavian traders who came down the Volga to sell furs and slaves for Arab silver. He admired their tall bodies and mocked their dirt, and he described in detail the funeral of a chieftain who was burned in his ship with a slave girl who was killed for the purpose. It is a key text for historians of the Rus and the Viking age.

The text was little known until a fuller manuscript was found in Mashhad in 1923.
